name: Sam Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m on a small building site outside Larchford by seven. I carry boards, mark and make rough cuts under Mara’s eye, and fix battens when she says the line is right. I came into building work three years ago after warehouse shifts dried up, so I’m still the junior man even at 58.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day do you like, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A straight row of battens you can see at the end of the day feels good. The lifting catches my shoulder, and a rainy week can mean fewer paid hours. My partner Ada cleans at a school part time; our grown children have their own bills, so I don’t count on them to cover ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I’d say the fancy software can keep its promises and let us get on with the walls. A phone can tally materials, but it can’t carry wet boards up a stairwell. My boss Mara still needs hands who turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I’d be relieved about the job, but I wouldn’t call our money safe. We rent, I’m on the lower rate, and we’ve got less than a month’s bills put by. A spell off for my shoulder would hurt us faster than any machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep taking the site shifts and ask Mara to show me the safer way to brace a frame. From the next payday I’d put a little aside before buying anything for the flat. If the small AI tally tool stays useful, I’ll let Mara use it; I don’t need to buy one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about work, still tight in the chest about the rent. I’ve learned not to treat a steady week as a steady year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first expense you would change if the site lost a week of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ada and I would cancel the extra mobile data first; that’s the easiest bill to move. We’ve already stopped taking the bus to see our daughter Nia every other weekend, which I hate. The rent comes before everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound relieved, but you are also saving more. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The machines leaving my work alone doesn’t make my shoulder younger. I left school early and there aren’t many other sites within a bus ride, so I want a little breathing room. I’m not saving for a grand retirement; I’m saving for the next missed shift.

say: I’d tell the crew **hands still matter** on a wet building site.
I’d say the material tally tool may save **Mara** some time.
think: I’d feel **relieved** about site work surviving.
I’d still fear **lost hours** or an injury with less than a month saved.
do: Keep taking **site shifts** and learn safer frame bracing from Mara.
Put aside money from the **next payday** for missed shifts.
feel: **Relief** about work, with rent anxiety still present.
S0.quote: I’m not saving for a grand retirement; I’m saving for the next missed shift.
fieldNote: His **shoulder** and uneven shifts threaten rent sooner than the modest software change on this card.
He wants Mara to teach **safer bracing** while he keeps taking site shifts.
His public confidence sits beside **thin savings** and the fear of another missed payday.

steps.text: Keep taking carpentry and general site shifts under Mara
Put money from the next payday aside for missed site shifts
Learn safer frame bracing from Mara during a site shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the office will change first. Mara may get schedules and timber orders from a screen, but someone still has to fit the boards around crooked walls. I’d push for the crew to hear about changes before our hours are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry the office will squeeze the timetable once software plans it, and the slowest pair of hands will be easiest to drop. I’m that junior pair more often than I like. Ada’s school may trim cleaning hours too if its budget gets tight, though I can’t know that from this card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d sit with Mara when she uses the materials list and learn to read it on the phone I own. I’d ask the site workers’ union representative about training and notice before changed shifts. In the first year of this change I’d keep a paper log of my hours and set aside each full week’s extra pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like someone has tightened the clock over our heads. I’m curious about the list tool, but curiosity won’t pay for a week they stop calling me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would learning the list tool change in your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could check how many battens are due before I start cutting, and spot when the sizes on paper don’t match the wall. Mara has to check my cuts anyway, but I could waste less timber. I used an AI phone answer once to work out a hinge size, then checked it with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you speak to first if the new schedule removed a shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mara first, with my own hours written down, because she decides who is called. If it hit the whole crew, I’d go with the others to our union representative. I don’t want one man begging quietly while the same thing happens to six of us.

say: I’d tell coworkers **site fitting** still needs people.
I’d ask for **early notice** before software changes the crew’s hours.
think: I may be the **junior worker** dropped when schedules tighten.
Ada’s **cleaning hours** could also shrink, though I cannot predict that.
do: Learn to read **material lists** with Mara on my phone.
Log every **paid hour** and ask the union representative about changed shifts.
feel: **Curious** about the tool and anxious about shorter weeks.
S1.quote: I don’t want one man begging quietly while the same thing happens to six of us.
fieldNote: He expects **office planning** to change first, but fears a tighter timetable could cost him shifts.
He tries a **materials list** on his own phone because it could prevent wasted timber.
He records hours and contacts the **union representative** in case cuts reach the whole crew.

steps.text: Learn to check site material lists on his own phone with Mara
Ask the site union representative about notice for changed shifts
Set aside extra pay from each full site week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that the thinking machine arrives in 2028 but it can’t fix a crooked wall then. The capable site robots come around 2031, and I’d want a public plan for workers before they roll in. I’d say we should speak together now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60 in 2028, I could still carry boards while AI does the orders and plans, but the boss might run a leaner crew already. By 2031 I’d be 63, and a robot doing the lifting and fitting could take the lower-paid junior slot I hold. Ada’s pay won’t cover the flat alone, and I have no guaranteed pension waiting at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d take my hours record to the union representative and ask for paid training or a bridge to retirement if robots replace us. I’d ask Mara to let me learn checking finished work, though I know I’m not qualified to inspect a whole building. In the first year after 2028 I’d keep site shifts, cut our extra spending, and bank every full week while the hands-on work is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be frightened enough to wake at night, but there is a sequence I can see. I’m not helpless in 2028; I’m afraid of what happens three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Imagine it is 2029 and the site is using AGI for planning. What would your workday look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d still be fixing battens and hauling boards, but Mara might get every measurement and delivery time from the system. I’d check the actual wall before cutting, because a perfect plan doesn’t flatten old plaster. If she stops calling one worker, I’d assume I’m in the running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you and Ada cut first if your paid hours fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d drop the trip to see Nia and the extra mobile data, then ask the landlord for time before we missed rent. I’d ask Ada whether she can take one more school cleaning shift, but her back is sore as well. I hate that our plan puts another load on her.

say: I’d tell the crew **AI plans** in 2028 while people still fit the walls.
I’d call for a **worker plan** before site robots arrive around 2031.
think: My **junior site role** may disappear when capable robots arrive.
Ada’s income cannot cover rent, and I have **no guaranteed pension** at 63.
do: Bring my **hours record** to the union representative this month.
Keep site shifts after 2028 while cutting **extra spending** and banking full weeks.
feel: **Frightened** about 2031, with a little control before then.
S2.quote: I’m not helpless in 2028; I’m afraid of what happens three years later.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 planning** changes from capable site robots arriving around 2031.
His **junior slot** looks vulnerable once robots can lift and fit; Ada’s wages cannot cover rent alone.
He seeks a **union bridge** and practical checking skills while continuing paid site work.

steps.text: Ask the site union representative for paid training or a retirement bridge
Ask Mara to teach him how to check completed site work
Keep taking site shifts during the first year after 2028
Cancel extra mobile data and family trips if site hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell people five years gives us time to bargain and learn, though it isn’t forever. AI could run the plans in 2031, and the hands-on robots come about 2034. I’d want the firm to train the crew before it buys machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2031 I’d be 63, and I could probably still earn on the tools while software handles planning. By 2034 I’d be 66, near the age I hoped to step back, but I cannot count on a pension cheque. Hope is not a pension cheque. I’d be safer than in the quick version only if I saved and kept my body working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d start a small weekly transfer from each paid week and ask Ada to review our rent and bills with me each month. This year I’d enrol in a short evening course on site safety and measuring, if the fee is manageable or the union helps. In the first year after 2031, I’d keep fitting and checking work while asking Mara how many years the crew has before robots do those parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It’s anxious rather than sleepless panic. Five years lets me count paydays, but a shoulder can put paid to a tidy plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course let you do that you cannot do today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could read drawings and check basic dimensions without making Mara stop her own work every ten minutes. It would not make me a qualified surveyor. If the site needs a person to spot an uneven wall after the AI draws it straight, I want to be useful there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Suppose it is 2032 and you are still fitting timber. What would you ask Mara then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask whether she expects robots for lifting or for the whole fitting job by 2034, and whether she’ll keep any human crew. I’d show her the course certificate and the measurements I’ve kept. If she says the hours will go, I’d ask the union about support before I leave, not just walk out.

say: I’d say **five years** allows bargaining and learning before AGI plans sites.
I’d ask the firm for **crew training** before robots arrive around 2034.
think: I could still earn at **63** while AI handles plans.
At **66**, robot replacement could beat my savings to retirement.
do: Transfer money from each **paid week** and review bills with Ada monthly.
Take a short **safety and measuring course** if the fee is manageable.
feel: **Anxious** about income, with time to prepare.
S3.quote: Hope is not a pension cheque.
fieldNote: Five years give him **paydays to save**, provided his shoulder lets him keep working.
He considers a **safety course** only if the fee is manageable or the union helps.
He hopes to check basic dimensions without claiming the authority of a **qualified surveyor**.

steps.text: Transfer a small amount from every paid site week into savings
Enrol in an affordable evening course on site safety and measuring
Keep fitting timber during the first year after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew a decade is enough to make a proper plan if the firm shares the gains. AI handling plans in 2036 may change Mara’s office work, but robots doing our fitting arrive around 2039. The younger workers would still need a fair path in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 68 when AGI arrives in 2036, and 71 when the robots catch the hands-on work. I hope I’m no longer climbing stairs with boards by then, but there’s no fixed pension date or payout I can rely on. Ada and I might need my wages past 68 if the rent keeps rising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep the job, take the basic measuring course, and build savings on every full week. Over the next decade Ada and I would set an actual monthly number we need before I reduce shifts. In 2037, the first year after AGI, I’d ask Mara for lighter checking and preparation work if my shoulder allows it, while the crew still fits by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More room to breathe, but I don’t feel settled. The dates give me time; they don’t fill a savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire before the robots arrive in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the sums work. I’d like to be done with lifting by 68, but I may need lighter paid work into my seventies. Calling it retirement without income would just be losing a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children about this longer timetable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Nia and Kojo to keep their own savings and choose training that leaves them options, not to pay our rent. I’d also tell them workers should have a voice in the change, because a machine can be useful and still leave a household short. They’ve heard me say that before.

say: I’d say **ten years** gives workers time if the firm shares the gains.
I’d defend a **fair entry path** for younger site workers.
think: At **68**, I may still need wages after AGI handles planning.
At **71**, robots could end hands-on work after I hope to stop lifting.
do: Keep the job and build **weekly savings** toward a real monthly target.
Ask Mara for **lighter checking work** in 2037 if my shoulder permits.
feel: **Breathing room** tempered by uncertainty about rent and retirement.
S4.quote: Calling it retirement without income would just be losing a wage.
fieldNote: He refuses to treat **age 68** as proof that paid work will no longer be needed.
The longer robot lag gives him time to seek **lighter checking work** from Mara.
He and Ada need a **monthly income target** before he can reduce shifts.

steps.text: Keep taking site shifts while he can manage the lifting
Save from full site weeks toward a monthly retirement income target
Complete the basic site measuring course before 2036
Ask Mara for lighter checking and preparation work in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 AGI one worries me most because I’d be 60 and the robots could take my site work at 63, before I could save enough to stop. Paid training that I can reach by bus, clear notice of changed hours, and a bridge payment if a whole crew is displaced would help. I want the union at that table, not a promise on a poster.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays while someone learns. A course after a long day is possible; a course that takes away a paid day is much harder for me. Ada and I live on both wages, and neither of us can promise the children a bill won’t come due.

headlineQuote: A course after a long day is possible; a course that takes away a paid day is much harder for me.
portrait: **Sam**, 58, is a late entrant to low-paid site carpentry with a sore shoulder.
He and Ada rely on **two wages** and have less than a month of expenses saved.
He tries small tools and training once he sees **practical use**.
He fears the **2028 path** because robots could reach his hands-on work at 63.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI path** could remove Sam’s site income when robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid training** reachable by bus and clear notice of changed shifts.
He wants a **bridge payment** and union voice if the crew is displaced.
